concepts.name: Laboratory safety and hazard symbols
concepts.description: Causes of laboratory accidents (fire, fumes, acids and alkalis, microorganisms, misuse of apparatus, electricity) and how to prevent them; laboratory rules, fire drills, emergency procedures and use of a first-aid kit; hazard symbols and safety labels on containers (e.g. corrosive, flammable, toxic, harmful or irritant, oxidising, hazardous to the environment). ZIMSEC 8.1.1 and 8.12.1; for Cambridge it supports the practical papers (hazards and safety precautions; the hazard codes listed in the syllabus are not assessed).

concepts.name: Branches of biology and careers
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (8.1.2, 8.1.3): the branches of biology (cytology, anatomy, physiology, ecology, genetics, biotechnology, microbiology, zoology, botany) and what each studies; careers that use biology, such as medicine, research science, ecology and conservation, and dietetics, and others such as nursing, pharmacy, agriculture, veterinary science and food technology.

concepts.name: Planning investigations
concepts.description: Independent, dependent and controlled variables; fair tests and control experiments; choosing a suitable range and number of values, apparatus and techniques; repeats and replicates; hypotheses and reasoned predictions; risks and safety precautions; writing a clear step-by-step method. Applied to the practical contexts of both syllabuses: diffusion, osmosis, food tests, enzymes, photosynthesis, transpiration, respiration, germination, tropisms, heart and breathing rates, soils.

concepts.name: Recording, presenting and evaluating results
concepts.description: Reading instruments to a suitable precision; results tables (quantity / unit headings, no units in the body, consistent decimal places); line graphs, bar charts and histograms (axes, scales, plotting, best-fit lines); calculations (mean, range, percentage change, rate, magnification of a drawing); interpolation and gradients; anomalous results; conclusions justified by data; sources of error, accuracy and reliability, and improvements; representative and random sampling; clear labelled biological drawings.

concepts.name: Characteristics of living organisms
concepts.description: Cambridge 1.1: the seven characteristics of living organisms (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition) with precise meanings, e.g. growth as a permanent increase in size and dry mass and excretion as removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements; using them to decide whether something is alive.

concepts.name: Classification, species and dichotomous keys
concepts.description: Cambridge 1.2: grouping organisms by shared features; a species as a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring; the binomial system (genus and species, e.g. Zea mays, Homo sapiens); constructing and using dichotomous keys from identifiable features. Supplement: classification reflects evolutionary relationships, DNA base sequences are used to classify, and closer relatives have more similar sequences.

concepts.name: The five kingdoms, plant groups and viruses
concepts.description: Main features used to place organisms in the animal and plant kingdoms (Cambridge Core); the five kingdoms (animals, plants, fungi, prokaryotes, protoctists) and their diagnostic features (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC 8.9.1 names them Prokaryotae or Monera, Protoctista or Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia); the plant groups ferns and flowering plants, with monocotyledons and dicotyledons (Cambridge Supplement); features of viruses (protein coat and genetic material) and why they are not placed in a kingdom.

concepts.name: Vertebrate and arthropod groups
concepts.description: Cambridge 1.3 Core: the main features of the vertebrate groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and of the arthropod groups (insects, arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods), and classifying unfamiliar animals from descriptions, drawings or photographs.

concepts.name: Plant, animal and bacterial cells
concepts.description: Structures of plant and animal cells (cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, chloroplasts, ribosomes, mitochondria, vacuoles), their functions and how plant and animal cells differ; structure of a bacterial cell (cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmids); identifying structures in diagrams and micrographs; new cells come from the division of existing cells. ZIMSEC 8.3.1: the cell as the unit of structure and function, the nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, vacuole, cell wall, mitochondrion and chloroplast, and observing and drawing cells seen with a microscope or bioviewer.

concepts.name: Specialised cells and levels of organisation
concepts.description: How the structure of specialised cells suits their functions: ciliated cells, root hair cells, palisade mesophyll cells, neurones, red blood cells, sperm and egg cells (Cambridge), with white blood cells and muscle cells (ZIMSEC 8.3.2); the levels of organisation cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism, with examples (Cambridge).

concepts.name: Magnification and the size of specimens
concepts.description: Cambridge 2.2: magnification = image size ÷ actual size, rearranged to find the actual size or the image size; measuring images in millimetres; scale bars; Supplement: converting between millimetres and micrometres (1 mm = 1000 μm); magnification of biological drawings in practical work.

concepts.name: Diffusion and active transport
concepts.description: Diffusion as the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration (down a concentration gradient) as a result of their random movement, using their kinetic energy; its importance for gases and solutes in organisms; factors affecting its rate (surface area, temperature, concentration gradient, distance) and investigations such as coloured agar cubes; active transport as movement against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration; Supplement: carrier proteins and the importance of active transport, e.g. ion uptake by root hairs. ZIMSEC uses these ideas for absorption ('diffusion and active uptake', 8.6.1), gas exchange and exchange between capillaries and tissue fluid.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.description: Water moving into and out of cells by osmosis through partially permeable membranes; investigations with dialysis (Visking) tubing and with plant tissue such as potato in solutions of different concentrations, including percentage change in mass; plants supported by water pressure inside cells; Supplement: water potential, turgid, turgor pressure, flaccid and plasmolysis, and the importance of osmosis in water uptake and loss by organisms; effects on animal cells. ZIMSEC: the syllabus does not name osmosis; the concept is covered under plant transport (8.5.3) to explain water uptake, turgor and wilting.

concepts.name: Water in living organisms
concepts.description: Water as a solvent in digestion, excretion and transport (Cambridge 3.2); the composition of water and how its properties (solvent, transparency, high specific heat capacity) relate to its roles in photosynthesis, temperature regulation and as a habitat (ZIMSEC 8.2.1).

concepts.name: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
concepts.description: Elements in carbohydrates, fats and oils (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen) and proteins (also nitrogen); large molecules built from smaller ones: starch, glycogen and cellulose from glucose, proteins from amino acids, fats and oils from fatty acids and glycerol. ZIMSEC (8.2.3, 8.13.1 to 8.13.3) adds classifying carbohydrates as monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides and the functions of carbohydrates, proteins (e.g. enzymes, structure, transport, antibodies) and lipids (e.g. energy store, cell membranes, insulation).

concepts.name: Food tests
concepts.description: Iodine solution test for starch, Benedict's test for reducing sugars (heated; colour from blue through green and yellow to orange or brick-red), biuret test for proteins, ethanol emulsion test for fats and oils and (Cambridge only) the DCPIP test for vitamin C: method, safety, positive and negative results, controls, and interpreting results for local foods.

concepts.name: Nucleic acids and the structure of DNA
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement (4.1): DNA as two strands coiled into a double helix, held together by bonds between pairs of bases that always pair A with T and C with G (full names not required), including working out complementary base sequences. ZIMSEC: the elements and nucleotide units of nucleic acids (8.2.3) and the roles of DNA and RNA in inheritance and protein synthesis (8.13.4).

concepts.name: Enzymes and how they work
concepts.description: Catalysts; enzymes as proteins that act as biological catalysts in all metabolic reactions, keeping reaction rates high enough to sustain life; the active site with a shape complementary to its substrate (the lock-and-key model) and the formation of products; specificity; Supplement: the enzyme-substrate complex; investigating enzyme properties, e.g. catalase breaking down hydrogen peroxide and amylase digesting starch (ZIMSEC 8.4.1).

concepts.name: Effects of temperature and pH on enzymes
concepts.description: Investigating and describing how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity: optimum temperature and pH, denaturation, measuring rates (e.g. time for starch to disappear using iodine, volume of oxygen released by catalase); Supplement: explanations in terms of kinetic energy, frequency of effective collisions, shape and fit of the active site and denaturation; interpreting rate graphs. ZIMSEC 8.4.2 (mode of enzyme action, lock-and-key).

concepts.name: Enzymes in industry and the home
concepts.description: Biological washing powders (proteases and lipases remove protein and fat stains at lower temperatures) and investigating them; pectinase in fruit juice production (Cambridge); Supplement: lactase to make lactose-free milk; advantages and limitations of using enzymes. ZIMSEC 8.14.1; Cambridge 21.2.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis
concepts.description: Photosynthesis as the making of carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using light energy transferred by chlorophyll in chloroplasts; the word equation and (Cambridge Supplement) the balanced equation 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; uses and storage of the carbohydrates made (starch, cellulose, glucose for respiration, sucrose for transport, nectar); investigating the need for chlorophyll, light and carbon dioxide with suitable controls (destarching, variegated leaves, the starch test on a leaf); the importance of photosynthesis in ecosystems (ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: Rate of photosynthesis and gas exchange in plants
concepts.description: Effects of light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis and investigating them (e.g. bubbles of oxygen from pondweed); limiting factors (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC 8.5.1) and interpreting rate graphs; gas exchange of plants in light and dark and the balance between photosynthesis and respiration, investigated with hydrogencarbonate indicator; stomata and their distribution (ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: Leaf structure
concepts.description: How leaves are adapted for photosynthesis: large surface area and thinness; the structures of a dicotyledonous leaf (cuticle, upper and lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, air spaces, guard cells and stomata, vascular bundles with xylem and phloem, chloroplasts) and how each helps photosynthesis and gas exchange; identifying them in diagrams and micrographs.

concepts.name: Mineral nutrition in plants
concepts.description: Mineral ions absorbed from the soil: nitrate for making amino acids and proteins and magnesium for chlorophyll (Cambridge 6.1); ZIMSEC 8.5.1: nitrogen (proteins, chlorophyll), phosphorus (ATP, nucleic acids) and potassium (ion and osmotic balance) and their deficiency signs (nitrogen: stunted growth, yellowing; phosphorus: stunted roots, purplish leaves; potassium: yellow or brown leaf margins, poor flowering); why farmers apply fertilisers.

concepts.name: Crop productivity, pests and diseases
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.5.2: biomass and productivity; factors affecting productivity (light, mineral salts, temperature, water, pests, diseases); tissue-eating and sap-sucking pests; plant diseases such as bacterial wilt and rust; how pests and diseases reduce yields; management, cultural, chemical and biological control and the advantages and disadvantages of each, with reference to crops such as maize, cotton and tobacco.

concepts.name: Nutrients and a balanced diet
concepts.description: A balanced diet; the main dietary sources and importance of carbohydrates, fats and oils, proteins, vitamins (C and D; ZIMSEC also A), mineral ions (calcium and iron; ZIMSEC also iodine), fibre and water; how energy and nutrient needs vary with age, sex and activity (ZIMSEC 8.6.1); scurvy and rickets as deficiency diseases (Cambridge 7.1).

concepts.name: Malnutrition and deficiency diseases
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.6.1: malnutrition as under-nutrition or over-nutrition; protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor, marasmus); deficiency diseases of vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin D and calcium, iron and iodine; effects of too much fat and carbohydrate (e.g. obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes); prevention through a varied diet and food fortification.

concepts.name: The digestive system
concepts.description: The organs of the alimentary canal (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine: duodenum and ileum, large intestine: colon, rectum, anus) and associated organs (salivary glands, pancreas, liver, gall bladder); their roles in ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion; peristalsis (ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: Teeth and physical digestion
concepts.description: Physical (mechanical) digestion and how it increases the surface area of food for enzymes; types of human teeth (incisors, canines, premolars, molars) and their functions; tooth structure (crown, neck, root; enamel, dentine, pulp cavity with nerves and blood vessels, cement; set in the jaw bone and gums); the stomach churning food; Supplement: bile emulsifying fats and oils; ZIMSEC 8.6.1: tooth decay caused by bacteria making acid from sugary food, plaque, and caring for teeth.

concepts.name: Chemical digestion and digestive enzymes
concepts.description: Chemical digestion of large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed; amylase, proteases and lipase: their substrates and products, where they are secreted and where they act; hydrochloric acid in gastric juice (kills microorganisms, gives the acidic pH for stomach enzymes); Supplement: amylase to maltose and maltase on the small-intestine lining, pepsin in the stomach and trypsin in the small intestine, bile neutralising the acidic mixture from the stomach; ZIMSEC 8.6.1 also lists rennin (clots milk protein) and bile emulsifying fats.

concepts.name: Absorption and assimilation
concepts.description: Absorption of digested food in the small intestine and of most water there (some in the colon); Supplement: villi and microvilli increase the surface area, the structure of a villus, capillaries and lacteals; ZIMSEC 8.6.1: adaptations of the small intestine (length, folding, villi, thin lining, rich blood supply), absorption by diffusion and active uptake, the hepatic portal vein, the roles of the large intestine, assimilation, and the liver's roles in metabolism (regulating glucose and amino acids, breaking down alcohol and toxins, storing glycogen, fat and vitamins A and D).

concepts.name: Xylem, phloem and water uptake
concepts.description: Functions of xylem (water and mineral ions, support) and phloem (sucrose and amino acids); positions of xylem and phloem in sections of roots, stems and leaves of non-woody dicotyledons; Supplement: xylem vessels with lignified walls, no cell contents and no cross walls; root hair cells and their large surface area; the pathway of water from root hair cells through the cortex and xylem to mesophyll cells, traced with a dye; ZIMSEC 8.5.3: external structure of a flowering plant, monocotyledons and dicotyledons compared, internal structure of roots and stems (epidermis, cortex, vascular tissue, pith).

concepts.name: Transpiration
concepts.description: Transpiration as loss of water vapour from leaves: evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces into air spaces and diffusion out through the stomata; its functions (moving water and ions up the xylem, cooling); effects of temperature, wind speed, humidity, light intensity, leaf surface area and stomatal distribution on its rate, investigated with a potometer, by loss of mass or with plastic bags; Supplement: internal surface area and stomata, transpiration pull drawing up a column of water held together by attraction between water molecules; wilting; ZIMSEC 8.5.3: leaf adaptations that reduce water loss (smaller surface area, thick cuticle, fewer or sunken stomata, hairs).

concepts.name: Translocation
concepts.description: Movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources (parts that release them, e.g. photosynthesising leaves, sprouting storage organs) to sinks (parts that use or store them, e.g. roots, fruits, growing points); why one part can be a source at one time and a sink at another (Cambridge Supplement only); ring-barking and its effects (ZIMSEC 8.5.3).

concepts.name: The heart and circulation
concepts.description: A circulatory system of blood vessels with a pump and valves; Supplement: the single circulation of a fish and the double circulation of a mammal and its advantages (ZIMSEC: pulmonary and systemic circulation); structures of the mammalian heart (muscular wall, septum, atria, ventricles, valves, coronary arteries); arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it; monitoring the heart (ECG, pulse, heart sounds); investigating the effect of physical activity on heart rate; Supplement and ZIMSEC: atrioventricular and semilunar valves, wall thickness of the chambers, the septum, the cardiac cycle and valve action.

concepts.name: Coronary heart disease and high blood pressure
concepts.description: Coronary heart disease as blockage of the coronary arteries; risk factors (diet, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, genetic predisposition, age, sex); the roles of diet and exercise in reducing the risk; ZIMSEC 8.6.5: causes of high blood pressure (e.g. inheritance, stress, lack of exercise, diet); interpreting data about risk factors.

concepts.name: Blood vessels
concepts.description: Structure of arteries, veins and capillaries (relative wall thickness, lumen diameter, valves in veins) and the functions of capillaries; Supplement and ZIMSEC: relating structure to blood pressure and function; the main vessels to and from the heart (vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein), lungs and kidneys (renal artery and vein) and (Supplement) liver (hepatic artery, hepatic veins, hepatic portal vein); ZIMSEC 8.6.5: exchange between capillaries and tissue fluid by diffusion and pressure filtration.

concepts.name: Blood
concepts.description: Components of blood (red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, plasma) and their functions: haemoglobin in red cells carries oxygen, white cells carry out phagocytosis and make antibodies, platelets in clotting, plasma transports blood cells, ions, nutrients, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide; identifying blood cells in photomicrographs and prepared slides; clotting prevents blood loss and the entry of pathogens; Supplement: lymphocytes and phagocytes, and clotting as fibrinogen changing to a fibrin mesh.

concepts.name: Pathogens, transmission and disease control
concepts.description: Pathogens and transmissible (infectious) diseases; direct transmission (blood and other body fluids) and indirect transmission (contaminated surfaces, food, water, animals, air); the body's defences (skin, hairs in the nose, mucus, stomach acid, white blood cells); controlling the spread of disease through a clean water supply, hygienic food preparation, personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment. ZIMSEC (8.11.1, 8.11.2): health as physical, mental, emotional and social well-being; personal, domestic and community hygiene, sanitation and health facilities; causes of disease (infection, genetic defects, chemicals, radiation, malnutrition, degeneration); infectious and non-infectious diseases (deficiency diseases, genetic diseases, cancer).

concepts.name: Immunity and vaccination
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement and ZIMSEC 8.6.6: body defences (ZIMSEC: skin, tears, clotting, white cells engulfing pathogens and making antibodies); antigens with specific shapes and antibodies with complementary shapes; active immunity after infection or vaccination; how vaccination works (weakened pathogens or their antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, memory cells) and how it controls the spread of disease; passive immunity from antibodies across the placenta and in breast milk, without memory cells; ZIMSEC: natural and artificial active and passive immunity (e.g. antiserum injections for snake bite and rabies), the Expanded Programme on Immunisation, and how HIV destroys white blood cells.

concepts.name: Cholera
concepts.description: Cholera as a disease caused by a bacterium and spread in water or food contaminated with faeces; Supplement: the toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine, water follows by osmosis, causing diarrhoea, dehydration and loss of ions from the blood; treatment by oral rehydration; prevention through safe water, sanitation and hygiene. Cambridge 10.1 (Supplement); ZIMSEC 8.11.2.

concepts.name: Malaria
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.11.2: malaria caused by the protoctist Plasmodium and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes (the vector); an outline of how the parasite passes between mosquito and human; symptoms; treatment and the problem of drug resistance; prevention and control (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, removing breeding sites, repellents, preventive medicines); why malaria risk is higher in hot, low-lying, wet areas.

concepts.name: Bilharzia (schistosomiasis)
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.11.2: bilharzia caused by Schistosoma blood flukes; an outline of the life cycle (eggs passed in urine or faeces, larvae infecting freshwater snails as the intermediate host, larvae released into water penetrating human skin); symptoms (e.g. blood in the urine, anaemia, damage to the bladder, intestines and liver); treatment; prevention (avoiding contact with infected water, using toilets, snail control, treatment programmes).

concepts.name: Tuberculosis and typhoid
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.11.2: tuberculosis as a bacterial disease spread by airborne droplets, its symptoms, its link with HIV, treatment with a long course of antibiotics, BCG vaccination and prevention; typhoid as a bacterial disease spread through contaminated food and water, its symptoms, treatment and prevention through sanitation and food hygiene.

concepts.name: The breathing system and ventilation
concepts.description: Parts of the breathing system (lungs, diaphragm, ribs, intercostal muscles, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and associated capillaries); features of gas exchange surfaces (large surface area, thin, moist, good blood supply, good ventilation); Supplement and ZIMSEC: the mechanism of breathing in and out (ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm, volume and pressure changes); Supplement: internal and external intercostal muscles, cartilage in the trachea, and goblet cells, mucus and ciliated cells protecting the airways.

concepts.name: Inspired and expired air, and breathing during exercise
concepts.description: Differences between inspired and expired air (oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapour; ZIMSEC also temperature), investigated with limewater; the effects of physical activity on the rate and depth of breathing (ZIMSEC also pulse rate), investigated and described; Supplement: explaining the differences in composition and explaining the breathing response by increased carbon dioxide in the blood detected by the brain.

concepts.name: Smoking and health
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.6.3: harmful substances in tobacco smoke (nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide, particles); short-term effects (damage to cilia, extra mucus) and long-term effects (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer) on the respiratory system, with reduced oxygen transport, addiction and heart disease; passive smoking; interpreting data on smoking and disease. (In the Cambridge syllabus smoking appears only as a risk factor for coronary heart disease.)

concepts.name: Respiration and aerobic respiration
concepts.description: Respiration as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy; uses of energy (muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses, keeping body temperature constant); aerobic respiration, its word equation and (Cambridge Supplement) the balanced equation C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O; ATP as the energy currency (ZIMSEC 8.6.4); investigating the effect of temperature on respiration in yeast.

concepts.name: Anaerobic respiration
concepts.description: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration; in yeast glucose → alcohol + carbon dioxide (Supplement: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂); in muscles during vigorous exercise glucose → lactic acid; muscle fatigue (ZIMSEC); Supplement and ZIMSEC: lactic acid and the oxygen debt, removed by a continued fast heart rate and deeper, faster breathing and by aerobic respiration of lactic acid in the liver.

concepts.name: Excretion: the kidneys and the liver
concepts.description: Excretion of carbon dioxide by the lungs and of urea, excess water and ions by the kidneys (ZIMSEC: also the skin); the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra; Supplement: cortex and medulla, the nephron (filtration in the glomerulus; reabsorption of all glucose, some ions and most water; urine formation), the liver assimilating amino acids into proteins and deaminating excess amino acids to form urea, and why urea must be excreted; ZIMSEC 8.16.2: kidney cortex, medulla and pelvis, renal blood vessels, kidney functions (urine formation, osmoregulation, pH regulation), kidney failure and dialysis.

concepts.name: The nervous system, reflexes and synapses
concepts.description: Electrical impulses travel along neurones; the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system; the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; the reflex arc (receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector) and reflex actions; a synapse as a junction between neurones; Supplement: synapse structure (vesicles of neurotransmitter, synaptic gap, receptor proteins), the events at a synapse and one-way transmission; ZIMSEC 8.16.3: the functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum, pituitary gland, hypothalamus and medulla oblongata.

concepts.name: The eye
concepts.description: Sense organs as groups of receptor cells responding to specific stimuli; the parts of the eye (cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, blind spot) and their functions; the pupil reflex; Supplement: antagonistic circular and radial muscles of the iris, accommodation (ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments, lens shape, refraction), rods and cones and their distribution, and the fovea; ZIMSEC 8.16.3: image formation and focusing, short sight and long sight and their correction.

concepts.name: The ear
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.16.3: structure of the human ear (pinna, ear canal, eardrum, ossicles, oval window, cochlea, semicircular canals, auditory nerve, Eustachian tube); how sound is transmitted to the cochlea and converted to impulses; the role of the semicircular canals in balance; looking after the ears.

concepts.name: Hormones and the endocrine system
concepts.description: A hormone as a chemical made by a gland and carried by the blood that alters the activity of target organs; endocrine glands and their hormones: adrenal glands and adrenaline, pancreas and insulin (and glucagon, Supplement), testes and testosterone, ovaries and oestrogen; adrenaline in 'fight or flight' (faster breathing and heart rate, wider pupils; Supplement: raising blood glucose); comparing nervous and hormonal control (speed and duration). ZIMSEC 8.16.4.

concepts.name: Tropisms and plant hormones
concepts.description: Phototropism and gravitropism (ZIMSEC: geotropism) as growth responses of shoots and roots to light and gravity, and investigating them; Supplement: chemical control of shoot growth by auxin (made in the shoot tip, diffusing through the plant, distributed unequally by light and gravity, stimulating cell elongation); ZIMSEC 8.15.2: plant hormones as chemicals made in one part and acting elsewhere (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene) and their commercial uses.

concepts.name: Homeostasis and blood glucose control
concepts.description: Homeostasis as keeping a constant internal environment; insulin lowers blood glucose concentration; Supplement: negative feedback around a set point, control of blood glucose by the liver with insulin and glucagon, and the treatment of Type 1 diabetes; ZIMSEC 8.16.4: the roles of insulin and glucagon, the signs and symptoms of diabetes mellitus (e.g. frequent urination, great thirst, tiredness, high blood glucose, glucose in the urine) and how it is managed.

concepts.name: Skin and body temperature control
concepts.description: Structures of the skin (hairs, hair erector muscles, sweat glands, receptors, sensory neurones, blood vessels, fatty tissue); keeping body temperature constant through insulation, sweating, shivering and the role of the brain (hypothalamus), and through vasodilation and vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying skin capillaries; negative feedback; responses in hot and cold conditions. Cambridge Supplement (14.4); ZIMSEC 8.16.2.

concepts.name: The skeleton, joints and movement
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.16.5: functions of the skeleton (support, protection, locomotion); the bones of the mammalian forelimb (scapula, humerus, radius, ulna) and hindlimb (pelvic girdle, femur, tibia, fibula); hinge and ball-and-socket joints and the movements they allow; antagonistic flexor and extensor muscles (e.g. biceps and triceps) moving a hinge joint.

concepts.name: Medicinal drugs and antibiotics
concepts.description: A drug as any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body; antibiotics treat bacterial infections but do not affect viruses; resistant bacteria reduce the effectiveness of antibiotics; Supplement: using antibiotics only when essential limits the development of resistant strains such as MRSA; ZIMSEC 8.21.1: medical uses of antibiotics (penicillin), analgesics (paracetamol, aspirin) and antimalarials, and the safe use of medicines.

concepts.name: Drug misuse
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.21.1: misuse of drugs such as alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and solvents; dependence (addiction) and withdrawal; physical, mental and social ill-effects (e.g. liver damage from alcohol, slower reactions and accidents, mental illness, family and financial problems); avoiding drug misuse and getting help.

concepts.name: Asexual and sexual reproduction
concepts.description: Asexual reproduction (one parent, genetically identical offspring) with examples from diagrams, images and information; ZIMSEC 8.15.1: natural vegetative reproduction (rhizomes, tubers, suckers, runners, bulbs) and artificial propagation (cuttings, grafting); sexual reproduction (fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote; genetically different offspring) and fertilisation; Supplement: haploid gametes and diploid zygotes; advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction for populations in the wild and for crop production (Supplement and ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: Flowers and pollination
concepts.description: Parts of an insect-pollinated flower (sepals, petals, stamens with filaments and anthers, carpels with stigma, style, ovary and ovules) and their functions; the anthers and stigmas of wind-pollinated flowers; differences between the pollen of insect- and wind-pollinated flowers and the structural adaptations of each type of flower; pollination as transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; Supplement and ZIMSEC: self-pollination and cross-pollination and their advantages and disadvantages (variation, adaptability, reliance on pollinators).

concepts.name: Fertilisation and germination in flowering plants
concepts.description: Fertilisation when a pollen nucleus fuses with a nucleus in an ovule; Supplement and ZIMSEC: growth of the pollen tube and its entry into the ovule; seeds and fruits forming after fertilisation; the conditions needed for germination (water, oxygen, a suitable temperature) and investigating them with controls; ZIMSEC 8.15.1: the roles of enzymes in germination (breaking down food stores, respiration).

concepts.name: Seed structure and dispersal
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.15.1: structure of a dicotyledonous seed (e.g. bean) and a monocotyledonous grain (e.g. maize): testa, hilum, micropyle, embryo with radicle and plumule, cotyledons, endosperm; why seeds and fruits are dispersed (colonising new areas, less overcrowding and competition, better survival); dispersal by wind, animals, water and self-dispersal (explosive pods), with adaptations and local examples.

concepts.name: Human reproductive systems and gametes
concepts.description: Parts and functions of the male reproductive system (testes, scrotum, sperm ducts, prostate gland, urethra, penis) and female reproductive system (ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina); fertilisation as fusion of the nuclei of a sperm and an egg cell; adaptive features of sperm (flagellum, mitochondria, enzymes in the acrosome) and egg cells (energy stores, jelly coat that changes at fertilisation); comparing male and female gametes (size, structure, motility, numbers); ZIMSEC 8.6.7: gamete formation (details of meiosis not required), the pathway of sperm and causes of infertility.

concepts.name: Fertilisation, pregnancy and the placenta
concepts.description: Fertilisation in the oviduct; the zygote forms an embryo, a ball of cells that implants in the lining of the uterus; functions of the umbilical cord, placenta, amniotic sac and amniotic fluid; Supplement: exchange of dissolved nutrients, gases and excretory products across the placenta, and pathogens and toxins that can cross the placenta and affect the fetus; ZIMSEC 8.6.7: development of the zygote, the roles and limitations of the placenta (maternal and fetal blood kept separate; antibodies, toxins and viruses such as HIV can cross), functions of amniotic fluid, and the dangers of drugs, smoking and alcohol in pregnancy.

concepts.name: Puberty, sex hormones and the menstrual cycle
concepts.description: Testosterone and oestrogen in the development and regulation of secondary sexual characteristics at puberty; the menstrual cycle in terms of changes in the ovaries and in the lining of the uterus; Supplement: where oestrogen and progesterone are produced in the cycle and in pregnancy, and the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in controlling the cycle and pregnancy; ZIMSEC 8.6.7: phases of the cycle, ovulation, fertile and infertile phases, and the roles of oestrogen and progesterone; interpreting cycle diagrams and hormone graphs.

concepts.name: Contraception
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.6.7: methods of contraception (abstinence, withdrawal, rhythm method, spermicides, condoms, diaphragms, intra-uterine devices, hormonal injections and pills, vasectomy, tubal ligation); how each prevents pregnancy; reliability, advantages and disadvantages; which methods also reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections.

concepts.name: Sexually transmitted infections and HIV/AIDS
concepts.description: A sexually transmitted infection (STI) as an infection passed on through sexual contact; HIV as a pathogen that causes an STI and may lead to AIDS; how HIV is transmitted and how the spread of STIs is controlled; ZIMSEC 8.6.7: bacterial and viral STIs (gonorrhoea, syphilis, chancroid, genital warts, genital herpes, HIV and AIDS), their causative agents, signs and symptoms, and control (abstinence, mutual faithfulness, condoms, contact tracing, treatment).

concepts.name: Chromosomes, genes and alleles
concepts.description: Chromosomes are made of DNA, which carries genetic information as genes; a gene as a length of DNA that codes for a protein; an allele as an alternative form of a gene; the inheritance of sex in humans with X and Y chromosomes; Supplement: haploid and diploid nuclei, and 23 pairs of chromosomes in human diploid cells; ZIMSEC 8.8.1 also introduces dominant and recessive alleles, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous.

concepts.name: Genes and protein synthesis
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement (17.1): the base sequence of a gene determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein and so its shape; DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins (enzymes, membrane carriers, receptors); an outline of protein synthesis (the gene stays in the nucleus, an mRNA copy is made and moves to the cytoplasm, ribosomes assemble amino acids in the order set by the mRNA bases); cells express only the genes for the proteins they need.

concepts.name: Mitosis and meiosis
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement (17.2, 17.3): mitosis as nuclear division giving genetically identical cells, its roles in growth, repair, replacement of cells and asexual reproduction, exact replication of chromosomes before it and separation of the copies during it; stem cells; meiosis as a reduction division (diploid to haploid) producing genetically different gametes. ZIMSEC mentions both only in human reproduction (gamete formation and development of the zygote; details not required).

concepts.name: Monohybrid inheritance
concepts.description: Inheritance; genotype and phenotype; homozygous, heterozygous and pure-breeding; dominant and recessive alleles (complete dominance); genetic diagrams and Punnett squares predicting monohybrid crosses, the F1 and F2 generations and phenotypic ratios of 3 : 1 and 1 : 1; interpreting pedigree diagrams; Supplement: test crosses to identify an unknown genotype; ZIMSEC 8.8.2 also treats sex determination by X and Y chromosomes as a cross.

concepts.name: Codominance and ABO blood groups
concepts.description: Codominance, in which both alleles in a heterozygote contribute to the phenotype; inheritance of the ABO blood groups (phenotypes A, B, AB and O; alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᵒ, with Iᴬ and Iᴮ codominant and both dominant to Iᵒ); genetic diagrams and ratios for crosses involving codominance. Cambridge Supplement (17.4); ZIMSEC 8.8.2.

concepts.name: Sex linkage
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement (17.4): a sex-linked characteristic is controlled by a gene on a sex chromosome and so is more common in one sex; red-green colour blindness as an example; genetic diagrams with alleles written on the X chromosome predicting phenotypes and ratios, including carrier females.

concepts.name: Continuous and discontinuous variation
concepts.description: Variation as differences between individuals of the same species; continuous variation (a range of phenotypes between two extremes, e.g. body length and mass; caused by genes and the environment) and discontinuous variation (a limited number of phenotypes with no intermediates, e.g. ABO blood groups, seed shape and colour in peas; usually caused by genes only); investigating, recording and graphing variation (histograms and bar charts); ZIMSEC 8.18.1 examples: leaf size, pod size, height, coat colour, mass, tongue rolling, sex.

concepts.name: Mutation
concepts.description: Mutation as genetic change and the way new alleles form; ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation; Supplement: gene mutation as a random change in the base sequence of DNA, and mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation as sources of genetic variation; ZIMSEC 8.8.3: gene mutations (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia, albinism), chromosome mutations (e.g. Down syndrome) and factors that increase mutation rates (radiation, carcinogens).

concepts.name: Adaptive features
concepts.description: Cambridge 18.2: an adaptive feature as an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment; interpreting images or information to describe the adaptive features of a species; Supplement: the adaptive features of hydrophytes and xerophytes.

concepts.name: Natural and artificial selection
concepts.description: Natural selection: genetic variation, production of many offspring, struggle for survival and competition, greater chance of reproduction for better-adapted individuals, which pass on their alleles; evolution (ZIMSEC 8.18.2); selective breeding (artificial selection) of crop plants and livestock over many generations, e.g. for productivity, quality and resistance to drought and disease; Supplement: adaptation as a result of natural selection, antibiotic-resistant bacteria as an example, and the differences between natural and artificial selection.

concepts.name: Food chains and food webs
concepts.description: Food chains as the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer; food webs; producers, consumers (primary to quaternary), herbivores, carnivores, decomposers and trophic levels; constructing and interpreting food chains and webs; human impacts through overharvesting and introduced species. Cambridge 19.2; ZIMSEC 8.10.2.

concepts.name: Energy flow and ecological pyramids
concepts.description: The Sun as the principal source of energy for biological systems; energy flow from light energy to chemical energy in organisms and its eventual transfer to the environment; energy lost along food chains (respiration, heat); pyramids of numbers and biomass and the advantages of pyramids of biomass; pyramids of energy (Cambridge Supplement; ZIMSEC 8.10.2); Supplement: why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient, why food chains usually have fewer than five trophic levels, and why it is more energy-efficient for humans to eat crops than livestock fed on crops.

concepts.name: The carbon cycle
concepts.description: The carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, decomposition, the formation of fossil fuels and combustion; how human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation affect the carbon dioxide concentration of the air. Cambridge 19.3; ZIMSEC 8.10.2.

concepts.name: The nitrogen cycle
concepts.description: Cambridge Supplement (19.3) and ZIMSEC 8.10.2: decomposition of plant and animal protein to ammonium ions, nitrification, nitrogen fixation by lightning and by bacteria (including those in the root nodules of legumes), absorption of nitrate ions by plants, making amino acids and proteins, feeding and digestion, deamination and denitrification; the roles of microorganisms.

concepts.name: Populations, communities and ecosystems
concepts.description: A population, a community and an ecosystem; factors affecting the rate of population growth (food supply, competition, predation, disease); the lag, exponential (log), stationary and death phases of a sigmoid population growth curve; interpreting population graphs; Supplement: explaining each phase, including limiting factors; ZIMSEC 8.20.1: carrying capacity and the limiting factors that set it (water, food, oxygen, space, shelter).

concepts.name: Ecosystems and soil
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.10.1: an ecosystem as a self-contained system of interdependent organisms and their physical environment, and its physical and biological components (air, water, soil, light, organisms); the biological components of soil (litter, earthworms, nematodes, termites, fungi, bacteria, humus) and their functions; clay, loam and sandy soils compared by experiment (particle size, aeration, water-holding capacity, drainage, leaching, pH).

concepts.name: Natural and artificial ecosystems and their management
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.10.3 and 8.20.1: artificial ecosystems compared with natural ones (species diversity) and the problems of limited diversity (reduced soil fertility, more pest problems); the advantages of ground cover (keeping topsoil, retaining water, reducing evaporation); harmful agricultural, mining, industrial and social activities and corrective measures; exceeding the carrying capacity of land, with degradation, overgrazing, disease and pollution.

concepts.name: Increasing food production
concepts.description: Cambridge 20.1: how agricultural machinery, chemical fertilisers, insecticides, herbicides and selective breeding have increased food production; the advantages and disadvantages of large-scale monocultures of crop plants and of intensive livestock production.

concepts.name: Habitat destruction and deforestation
concepts.description: Biodiversity as the number of different species living in an area; reasons for habitat destruction (land for housing, crops and livestock; extraction of natural resources; freshwater and marine pollution); how altering food webs harms habitats; the undesirable effects of deforestation (reduced biodiversity, extinction, loss of soil, flooding, more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere); ZIMSEC 8.19.1: threats to biodiversity, including deforestation, habitat destruction and invasive species.

concepts.name: Pollution of water and land
concepts.description: Effects of untreated sewage and excess fertiliser on aquatic ecosystems; Supplement: eutrophication (more nitrate and other ions, more growth of producers, more decomposition after they die, more aerobic respiration by decomposers, less dissolved oxygen, death of organisms that need it); effects of non-biodegradable plastics in water and on land; ZIMSEC 8.19.1: pollution as a threat to biodiversity.

concepts.name: The enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change
concepts.description: Sources of carbon dioxide and methane in the air (e.g. burning fossil fuels, deforestation, cattle, rice paddies, landfill and decomposing waste); the enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change and their effects on organisms and agriculture; ZIMSEC 8.19.1: climate change as a threat to biodiversity and the use of alternative sources of energy.

concepts.name: Conservation and sustainable resources
concepts.description: A sustainable resource as one produced as rapidly as it is removed; forests and fish stocks managed sustainably (Supplement: education, protected areas, quotas and replanting for forests; closed seasons, protected areas, controlled net types and mesh sizes, quotas and monitoring for fish); why organisms become endangered or extinct; conserving endangered species (monitoring and protection, education, captive breeding, seed banks; Supplement: artificial insemination and IVF in captive breeding, and the risks of reduced genetic variation); Supplement: reasons for conservation programmes; ZIMSEC 8.19.1: conservation measures such as afforestation (tree planting), alternative sources of energy and preserving endangered species.

concepts.name: Microorganisms in biotechnology
concepts.description: Why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification (rapid reproduction, ability to make complex molecules; Supplement: few ethical concerns and the presence of plasmids); anaerobic respiration of yeast in making ethanol for biofuels and in bread-making; ZIMSEC 8.7.1: yeast in bread and alcohol production, bacteria in making yoghurt, cheese and insulin, and fungi making penicillin; Supplement: fermenters for the large-scale production of insulin, penicillin and mycoprotein and the conditions controlled in them (temperature, pH, oxygen, nutrient supply, waste products).

concepts.name: Genetic modification
concepts.description: Genetic modification as changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes; examples (human genes in bacteria to make human proteins; crops made resistant to herbicides or insect pests or with improved nutritional qualities); Supplement: outline of making a human protein in bacteria (restriction enzymes, sticky ends, plasmids, DNA ligase, recombinant plasmids, multiplication and expression) and the advantages and disadvantages of genetically modified crops such as soya, maize and rice; ZIMSEC 8.17.1: recombinant DNA as DNA combining genes from different organisms, transfer of genes between species, insulin production and the benefits and hazards of the technology.

concepts.name: Microorganisms: viruses, bacteria and fungi
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.7.1: the main characteristics of viruses (protein coat and genetic material; reproduce only inside living cells), bacteria (cell wall, cytoplasm, no nucleus, circular DNA, plasmids; reproduce by binary fission) and fungi (hyphae and mycelium or single cells such as yeast; spores; saprotrophic or parasitic nutrition); their economic importance: decomposition and bioremediation, food and drink production and medicines, and harmful effects such as disease and food spoilage.

concepts.name: Livestock productivity and health
concepts.description: ZIMSEC 8.16.1: food conversion efficiency (the food eaten compared with the gain in mass) and factors affecting livestock productivity; animal pests and diseases such as anthrax (bacterial), foot-and-mouth disease (viral), liver fluke (a parasitic flatworm) and redwater (spread by ticks), how they reduce productivity, and their prevention and control by dosing, vaccination, dipping and quarantine.
